name: Škoda 110 Super Sport
hook: Škoda's one-off 1970s sports coupé had no ordinary doors, and ten years later it played a car that ran on its driver's blood.
story:
Picture a white wedge at a Kvasiny factory in 1971. It is the only one ever made.

This is the Škoda 110 Super Sport. Almost nothing about it works the way you expect.

The engine sits behind you. It is a little 1.1-litre four, borrowed from a Škoda rally saloon. Up front, where you might look for an engine, there is room for your luggage and the spare wheel.

Getting in is stranger still. There are no ordinary doors. The doors, the windscreen and the roof all tip up together, like a canopy. Six headlamps pop up from the nose as one block. At the back sit sixteen round lamps, said to look like the tail of a rocket.

The engineer Stanislav Cinkl spent a long time on it. Škoda showed it at the Brussels Motor Show in 1972. The planned economy did not, and it never went on sale.

Ten years later, a film studio painted it black. It became a horror film's car that ran on blood, not petrol. That is how most people know it now.
description: The 110 Super Sport, type 724, was a one-off prototype coupé built by Škoda at its Kvasiny plant in 1971 and shown at the 1972 Brussels Motor Show. It has a fibreglass body, a rear-mounted 1.1-litre four from the 110 L Rallye and rear-wheel drive, and weighs about 900 kg. It never reached production. In 1981 designer Theodor Pištěk restyled it in black as the Ferat Vampire RSR for Juraj Herz's film Upír z Feratu, and Škoda's museum keeps it today.
